analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks for multinational corporations that shift profits and jobs offshore.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat untouched in the Ways and Means Committee since February 2025 — 140 House Democrats back it, no Republican does, and there has been no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises taxes on large US multinational companies that report profits in low-tax foreign countries. It ends a special deduction that lets those companies pay a reduced rate on foreign profits, forces them to count offshore income country by country so low-tax-haven profits can't be blended away, limits their ability to load US companies with debt to shrink their US tax bill, and tightens the rules so a company can't escape US taxes by moving its paper headquarters abroad while being run from here. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit if offshore tax breaks close: fewer loopholes means more federal revenue and less of the burden falling on domestic workers and companies. US workers also gain if companies no longer get a tax discount for locating plants and profits abroad.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Section 250 deduction, which lets multinational companies pay a reduced rate on foreign profits and on foreign-derived intangible income, and instead requires them to include their net foreign tested income in US taxation each year.

It applies the tax and the foreign tax credit separately for each country where income is earned, so profits parked in low-tax havens can no longer be blended with taxes paid in high-tax countries to shrink the US bill.

It caps interest deductions for domestic corporations that are part of large international financial reporting groups, limiting the practice of shifting US taxable income away through debt placed on the US subsidiary.

It tightens the rules on corporate inversions — treating as domestic any company where former owners hold at least 80% of the stock or where management and control remain primarily in the United States — and treats foreign corporations that are managed and controlled from the US as domestic for income tax.

analysis.who_pays: Large US-headquartered multinational corporations that currently pay reduced rates on foreign income, use tax havens, load US subsidiaries with interest deductions, or have inverted on paper. Costs could be passed to shareholders or, in some cases, reflected in prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: US multinational corporations using offshore tax strategies

drawbacks.text: The changes apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, so companies would face new rules on income already in motion, with little time to adjust their structures.

The country-by-country rules and interest caps add compliance and reporting burdens for companies that operate in many countries, and critics argue they could tax foreign income at rates that leave US-headquartered firms paying more than foreign rivals operating in the same markets.

The measure to treat US-managed foreign corporations as domestic goes beyond inversions, reaching any sizable foreign company whose day-to-day decisions are made from the US, which companies argue creates double taxation on income also taxed where it is earned.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is a straightforward closing of offshore loopholes, and the heavier compliance load falls on large companies already producing consolidated financial statements and country-level data. The strongest honest objections are the competitiveness concern — that US multinationals could face higher effective taxes than foreign competitors — and the treatment of widely-held foreign companies managed from the US, which some would call overbroad. On balance the costs fall on corporations and their shareholders, while the gains are lower avoidance and more revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 5, 2025 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, and no further action appears in its record.
140 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans appear among the cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinational corporations that benefit from the current reduced rates on foreign income, tax-haven blending, and interest shifting keep those breaks for now, since the bill has not advanced in the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since its referral in February 2025 — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 140 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican chair of the tax-writing committee has not moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill repeals the reduced rate they pay on foreign profits and requires country-by-country counting of income and foreign taxes, raising their US tax bill. It also caps their ability to deduct interest on US subsidiaries of international groups.

industries.industry: Tax-haven jurisdictions and offshore profit-shifting structures
industries.note: Country-by-country application ends the ability to blend low-taxed haven income with high-taxed income elsewhere, removing much of the incentive to route profits through havens.

industries.industry: Companies pursuing tax inversions or US-managed foreign incorporation
industries.note: The bill tightens the inversion rules and treats foreign corporations managed and controlled from the United States as domestic, closing routes to shifting tax residence abroad while keeping operations and management here.
These companies already pay full rates on US income and get no offshore break, so closing the gaps reduces the competitive disadvantage created by rivals' offshore structures.

analysis.trajectory: With the Ways and Means Committee majority favoring extension of the 2017 tax provisions this bill rolls back, and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote this Congress unless control of the House changes or it is folded into a broader tax bill.
